title: Can Walmart's New Bundled Subscription Beat Amazon?
detail:
Can Walmart's New Bundled Subscription Beat Amazon?
Catie Hogan, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 25, 2026 at 9:47 AM PDT 3 min read
WMT
AMZN
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) is offering a bundled subscription deal that could knock Amazon's (NASDAQ: AMZN) Prime membership off its pedestal. Earlier this week, the company announced a combined Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus membership for just $120 per year. That's $100 less than the two programs priced separately, and $19 less than Amazon Prime's $139 cost.

The bundle includes free delivery, 2% Sam's Cash on select purchases, $0.10 off per gallon of gas, and a choice between Peacock and Paramount+ streaming, among other perks. The catch is that it is only available as an annual subscription, and there's no free trial or monthly option available at this time.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Memberships have proven to be lucrative revenue channels for companies like Walmart and Amazon. Shoppers tend to spend significantly more with the merchant when they have a membership, roughly four times as much as non-members in Walmart's case.

So can Walmart's new subscription bundle dethrone Amazon Prime? Probably not. Amazon Prime is so deeply entrenched at this point that the mix of streaming, fast shipping, and ubiquity among consumers is almost immovable. However, Walmart doesn't have to beat Amazon to succeed. This is what investors should focus on.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

This particular offering strengthens Walmart's flywheel and advertising business. Walmart stock trades at a hefty premium, leaving little room for stumbles this holiday season. Some investors may want to wait for a better entry point. Still, overall, Walmart is an incredibly strong business that just created a new product that will help solidify and deepen customer engagement.

Shares of Walmart have risen nearly 6% year to date as of this writing. The stock is trading at roughly 40 times both forward and trailing earnings. The company's e-commerce segment continues to grow substantially, increasing 23% in the fiscal 2027 second quarter. Walmart's membership growth was also impressive at 17%.

Whether it overtakes Amazon or not, Walmart is a worthy investment.

What is driving increased demand for credit default swaps?

Investors are increasing their use of credit default swaps (CDS) to hedge exposure to debt issued by companies involved in artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to market data and financial industry research.

The increase comes as technology companies raise substantial amounts of capital to finance data centres, semiconductors and other computing infrastructure.

Morgan Stanley Research reported that weekly trading in CDS linked to bonds issued by Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta (NASDAQ:META), Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) averaged more than $9 billion in September.

That compares with less than $2 billion per week in July.

Separately, Bloomberg data showed that trading volumes in US corporate CDS indices have already exceeded the total recorded throughout 2025.

The increase reflects greater demand for instruments that can provide protection against credit losses or allow investors to express views on changes in corporate credit risk.

How much debt have AI-related companies issued in 2026?

According to Morgan Stanley, AI-linked debt issuance reached an estimated $466 billion so far in 2026, compared with $101 billion during the corresponding period of 2025.

The increase has been driven by financing requirements for artificial intelligence infrastructure, including data centres, chips and associated computing systems.

Companies involved in developing and operating these facilities have accessed bond markets and other credit sources to support their investment programmes.

The expansion in borrowing has also increased investor attention on the relationship between upfront capital expenditure and the revenue that infrastructure projects may generate over time.

As debt issuance grows, investors are assessing how financing costs, operating performance and the financial relationships between AI companies could affect creditworthiness.

How do credit default swaps work?

A credit default swap is a financial derivative that provides protection against specified credit events, such as a default by a corporate borrower.

The buyer of protection makes payments to the seller in exchange for compensation if a covered credit event occurs, subject to the contract's terms.

CDS prices are generally expressed as a spread in basis points, with 100 basis points equivalent to one percentage point annually.

For example, a CDS spread of 108 basis points represents an annual premium of approximately $108,000 to protect $10 million of debt, assuming a conventional running-premium structure.

Prediction: Amazon Stock Will Skyrocket After Oct. 29 Thanks to AWS Growth
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

AMZN
^GSPC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) has been a poor stock to own recently. While it rose following its Q2 earnings release, the stock has slowly sold off since then and is now up about 8% for the year, trailing the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC). However, I think this could all turn around once again after Oct. 29, when Amazon reports Q3 earnings.

The reason is fairly clear, and investors have already seen it cause Amazon's price tag to spike once already this year: cloud computing growth.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Amazon is the industry leader in cloud computing

Amazon may not be the first name you think of when discussing huge tech companies, but it should be high on the list. While most consumers are familiar with Amazon's commerce site and delivery platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS) really steers the business. In fact, AWS -- which supplies cloud computing -- accounted for 60% of Amazon's operating income in Q2, despite making up only 21% of revenue.

How? AWS's operating margins are far superior to those of its commerce business, which is a notoriously razor-thin-margin industry.

While commerce still affects Amazon's investment picture, investors must realize that Amazon doesn't care much about it right now. Amazon is spending about $220 billion this year to expand its computing infrastructure and fuel AWS growth. It seems content with its current dominance in commerce and sees a major opportunity in cloud computing right now, thanks to booming demand for running AI workloads.

These investments have so far paid off, as AWS's growth rate has significantly climbed over the past few quarters. Rewinding to Q4 2025, AWS's growth was 24% year over year. Then it accelerated to 28% in Q1 2026. Amazon surprised investors by reporting impressive 37% growth in Q2, which caused shares to skyrocket earlier this year before eventually selling off.

If Amazon continues to meaningfully accelerate its AWS growth rate, say to the mid-40% range, it could ignite another run-up in stock price, as it would have a positive effect on Amazon's operating margins. This, in turn, will cause earnings per share to rise faster, which the market will love.

If it can do that, Amazon's stock should be primed to rise, because it's actually pretty reasonably valued right now, at least compared to historical levels.
